A build-along course

Building Sextant

Logs, traces and metrics, and a query language to ask them questions. Not a wrapper around somebody else's engine: a hand-written lexer, a Pratt parser, a type checker that knows a duration is not a number, an evaluator, and a planner that pushes what it can into SQL and is honest about the rest. Built from an empty folder, with every bug found along the way written down.

Everything we'll cover

  1. 01 What we are building Sextant: a self-hosted observability platform — logs, traces, metrics, and a query language of our own to ask them questions.
  2. 02 Why a query language, and what it must refuse The four things a search box cannot do, the three properties a language for telemetry needs, and the decision to make units part of the type system.
  3. 03 The toolchain, and one config file Node, pnpm, SvelteKit 3, Vite, Vitest and Playwright — and why SvelteKit 3 has no svelte.config.js.
  4. 04 The environment, declared once `defineEnvVars`, valibot schemas that run at boot, and the four numbers that decide whether this survives a bad day.
  5. 05 Tokens, and why every one carries a position The vocabulary of SQF, and the single decision — a span on every token — that makes every error message in the language point at a column.
  6. 06 The lexer A hand-written scanner: why not regular expressions, how a duration differs from a number, and why an unterminated string must not eat the rest of the query.
  7. 07 The syntax tree A source and a pipeline of stages — and why pipelines rather than SQL’s clause order is the decision that makes completion possible.
  8. 08 The Pratt parser One loop and a table instead of six near-identical functions — and the guard that was written in the wrong place and could never fire.
  9. 09 Errors that point at something One error type for the whole front end, the difference between a message and a hint, and did-you-mean by edit distance.
  10. 10 The schema: what a column is, and what a function promises Three tables, a function table, and the parameter type that exists solely to make one error message lead somewhere.
  11. 11 The type checker Scope threading through pipeline stages, aggregates that may only appear in `summarize`, and units as a type error.
  12. 12 Values, and three-valued logic What `null` means in a query language, why `false and null` is `false`, and the one place comparison coerces a numeric string.
  13. 13 The evaluator Rows in, rows out, one stage at a time — plus the regex cache, the truncation flag, and why `summarize` builds its groups in one pass.
  14. 14 Testing an evaluator against a reference Differential testing: a naive implementation nobody would ship, used as an oracle for the one we do.
  15. 15 DDSketch: percentiles you are allowed to merge Why you cannot average a p95, what relative error means, and the log-bucket trick that makes a percentile cost a few kilobytes.
  16. 16 HyperLogLog: counting things you cannot hold Estimating distinct counts in 2KB, the avalanche finaliser that makes it work, and the small-cardinality correction that makes it usable.
  17. 17 Buckets, steps and rollups A fixed ladder of steps where every rung divides the next, absolute rather than now-relative boundaries, and the gap a chart must draw as a gap.
  18. 18 LTTB: keeping the shape Why averaging a series to fit a chart destroys the thing you are looking for, and how largest-triangle-three-buckets keeps real samples.
  19. 19 Assembling a trace from spans that arrive in any order Four things that are true of real trace data, each of which breaks the obvious implementation — and the four fixes, each a few lines.
  20. 20 The alert state machine `for` duration, hysteresis, and the one case that decides whether an alerting system is trustworthy: no data is not zero.
  21. 21 The schema, and the indexes that decide everything Three tables of telemetry, one composite index that every query uses, and two timestamps that must never be conflated.
  22. 22 Ingest: streamed, bounded, idempotent Reading a body without buffering it, refusing before parsing, and a unique index that makes a retry free.
  23. 23 Cardinality, and the NUL byte that ate every series A series key built from labels, a limit that has to be per metric, and a separator that SQLite quietly truncated at.
  24. 24 Storage: pushdown, and the rule for when not to Compiling a predicate to SQL when — and only when — SQL’s answer is identical, including nulls.
  25. 25 Sessions for people, keys for machines Two authentication paths that never meet, 404 versus 403, and why an API key is hashed with SHA-256 rather than bcrypt.
  26. 26 Live tail: backpressure as a feature Server-sent events with a bounded buffer, a dropped count that is shown rather than logged, and the ping that stops a proxy killing the stream.

Every code block in this course is read out of the finished project in sextant at build time — file and line numbers included — so it cannot drift from what the code actually says. Type it out rather than pasting where you can: the errors you make and fix are the part that sticks. A dozen chapters end with a bug that was genuinely in this codebase, what it looked like from the outside, and how it was cornered.
